strengths: Novel problem formulation: First systematic study of action-level backdoor attacks on TO models, identifying the critical gap that reward manipulation is ineffective for behavior cloning-based models
Thorough empirical investigation: Comprehensive analysis of key factors (target action selection, trigger design, reward manipulation) with well-designed ablation studies and multiple random seeds
Strong empirical results: 71.9% ASR with only 0.3% poisoning rate represents 105% improvement over Baffle and 27.2% over IMC, with excellent stealth (0.914 BTP)
Comprehensive evaluation: 972 experiments across 6 environments, 3 TO models, 3 target action types with careful ablations and robustness tests
Well-motivated technical approach: Each component (trajectory filtering, batch poisoning, alternating training) is clearly justified and shown necessary through ablations
Excellent reproducibility: Code available, detailed hyperparameters, clear algorithm specification, thorough experimental setup documentation
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Core components are straightforward applications—trajectory filtering (simple length-based), batch poisoning (poison 1 transition), alternating training (from existing IMC work). Novelty primarily in problem identification rather than technical innovation

Critical unsolved problem—trigger dimension selection: Paper shows dimensions critically affect success (Table 2: 0.91→0.0 ASR variance) but provides no principled selection method. Appendix F shows gradient-based approaches (Grad-CAM, NTK) don't correlate with effectiveness. Hardcoded to (1,2,3) limits generalization

Target action difficulty not characterized: Table 1 shows 0.11→1.0 ASR variance across action types; Table 17 shows 'arithmetic' targets are harder (0.536 CP vs 0.942 for '1'). No framework for predicting difficulty or understanding transferability

Incomplete baseline evaluation: Only Baffle and IMC compared; IMC from adversarial input literature, not designed for TO models. Anomalously low baseline CP values (e.g., 0.013) unexplained, raising fairness concerns
No defense analysis or mechanisms: Limitation A.3 briefly dismisses reward-based defenses but provides no systematic defense analysis or proposed countermeasures, limiting practical applicability

Lack of theoretical insight: Primarily empirical; no formal analysis of why/when TrojanTO succeeds. Why do certain state dimensions enable attacks? What TO model properties are exploited? No theoretical guarantees

Limited real-world applicability: All experiments in simulation (D4RL). Threat model assumes full training-time access (strong assumption). No analysis of deployment detection, trigger embedding stealth in practice, or real-world validation

Evaluation metric details: ASR success threshold ε not prominently specified; CP metric somewhat ad-hoc; 100 evaluation episodes may be insufficient for high-dimensional continuous control; normalization by clean policy could be problematic

strengths: Identifies important gap: demonstrates that existing reward-manipulation-based RL backdoor attacks fail on TO models, revealing a real security vulnerability in trajectory optimization models
Comprehensive empirical investigation: systematic analysis of key factors (target action selection, trigger design, reward manipulation) in Section 3 provides valuable insights

Strong experimental evaluation: consistent improvements over baselines (0.701 CP vs 0.342 Baffle, 0.551 IMC), tested across 3 models, 6 environments, multiple target actions, with thorough ablation studies
Well-motivated design: the three components (trajectory filtering, batch poisoning, alternating training) are clearly justified with good intuition for why they help
Reproducibility: detailed appendices with hyperparameters, algorithm specification, and implementation details; promised code release
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: trajectory filtering is simple data preprocessing, batch poisoning is standard, and alternating training directly applies existing Input Model Co-optimization (IMC); contribution is mainly combining known techniques for a new setting

Fundamental unsolved problems acknowledged but unresolved: (1) trigger dimension selection has extreme performance variance (0.915 vs 0.000) with no automated selection method despite extensive exploration; (2) target action difficulty varies 9x (0.11 to 1.0) with no principled characterization

No defensive contributions: paper explicitly acknowledges existing reward-based defenses are ineffective but provides no mitigation strategies, alternative defenses, or detection methods - purely offensive work

Insufficient mechanistic understanding: beyond empirical demonstration that reward manipulation doesn't work (Figure 1), lacks deeper analysis of why TO models are fundamentally different or theoretical characterization of vulnerabilities

Strong threat model assumptions: requires adversary control over training process; deployed/frozen models may be inaccessible; no experiments on realistic data validation or anomaly detection scenarios

Questionable design choices lack justification: (1) trajectory filtering by length lacks principled justification and is dataset-dependent; (2) single-transition batch poisoning seems to dilute signal with no full-batch ablation; (3) switching to model-only updates after M//2 iterations unmotivated

Evaluation issues: ASR threshold ε not clearly specified in main text, no sensitivity analysis to ε, suspicious zero standard deviations in Table 7, no statistical significance testing despite multiple runs

Under-explored hyperparameter sensitivity: many hyperparameters (λ, μ, α, trigger bounds) with limited ablation; task-specific tuning suggests limited generalization; alternation frequency ablation only in appendix
Persistent backdoor limitations inadequately discussed: Table 6 shows degradation over time, performance limited to <20 steps due to context window - significant practical constraints
Limited baseline comparisons: only Baffle and IMC compared; Baffle not designed for TO models; missing stronger analysis of why other approaches fail; no comparison to simpler alternatives

strengths: Novel problem identification: First action-level backdoor attack against TO models, addressing an important gap between reward-based RL attacks and action-reconstruction-based TO models

Comprehensive empirical investigation: Systematic analysis of key factors (target actions, trigger dimensions, reward manipulation) with clear demonstrations that existing approaches are ineffective (Section 3)

Extensive experimental evaluation: 6 D4RL environments, 3 TO architectures, 3 target action types, rigorous ablations showing 105% improvement over Baffle and consistent robustness across diverse settings
Well-motivated methodology: Three components (trajectory filtering, batch poisoning, alternating training) are clearly justified with thorough ablations confirming individual contributions
Strong empirical results: 71.9% ASR with only 0.3% poisoning rate while maintaining 91.4% benign task performance demonstrates practical attack efficiency
Excellent reproducibility: Code promised, detailed hyperparameters documented, training resources specified, results averaged over multiple seeds
weaknesses: Unresolved trigger dimension selection: Despite identifying this as critical (Table 2), the paper provides no principled solution. Attempted Grad-CAM and NTK methods failed. Current approach fixes dimensions (1,2,3) without justification, limiting practical applicability

Limited algorithmic novelty: Components are straightforward applications of existing techniques (simple length-based trajectory filtering, standard batch poisoning, alternating training adapted from IMC [24]). Contribution is primarily in problem identification rather than methodological innovation

Missing defense mechanisms: Paper acknowledges reward-based defenses are ineffective but proposes no countermeasures, detection strategies, or defenses. For a security paper, this gap significantly limits practical impact and actionability

Design choices lack justification: Algorithm 1 switches to model-only updates after M/2 iterations without explanation. Trajectory length threshold is arbitrary. Harmonic mean (CP) assumes equal ASR/BTP weighting despite different real-world priorities

Incomplete failure mode analysis: Performance varies dramatically across settings (CP ranges 0.0-1.0 in Table 17). 'Arithmetic' targets much harder than '1' with limited explanation. High variance in some settings (e.g., Hopp fixed random: CP = 0.121±0.121)

Evaluation concerns: Some results show BTP > 1.0 (Table 4, GDT Walk: 1.089), suggesting backdoor improves performance—needs explanation. ASR threshold ε choice not discussed or justified with sensitivity analysis
Threat model limitations: Assumes post-training model modification access. Limited analysis of detectability through behavioral testing or how practitioners could identify poisoned models in practice
Sparse persistent backdoor evaluation: Section 5.3 uses only 3 environments. Context window limitation (K≤20) underexplored despite being important practical constraint

strengths: First systematic study of action-level backdoors against TO models, addressing an important and timely security gap
Valuable empirical insights on critical factors: target action selection and trigger design matter, while reward manipulation is ineffective
Highly practical post-training attack achieving 0.719 ASR with only 0.3% poisoning rate, significantly outperforming Baffle (0.369 ASR with 10%)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 6 D4RL environments, 3 TO model architectures, diverse target actions, with extensive ablations and multiple seeds
Well-maintained benign task performance (0.914 BTP) while achieving high attack success, demonstrating good stealth
Reproducible research with provided code and detailed hyperparameters in supplementary materials
Honest evaluation of existing defenses, revealing that standard methods fail for continuous action spaces
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components (trajectory filtering, batch poisoning, MI-FGSM alternating training) are adapted from existing work; primary contribution is application to new model class rather than methodological innovation

Critical unsolved problem: trigger dimension selection is highly sensitive (Table 2: 0.915 vs 0.000 ASR), but gradient-based methods (Grad-CAM, NTK spectrum) fail to predict good dimensions; no principled selection method provided

Weak treatment of defenses: paper demonstrates vulnerabilities but only fine-tuning works (requiring retraining), and no novel defense mechanisms are proposed—ethically concerning for a security paper

Incomplete practical analysis: persistent backdoors limited to ~20 timesteps by context window; applicability to vision-based observations unaddressed; trigger injection mechanisms for real systems unclear
Target action selection problem unresolved: significant performance variation across action types (0.536 CP for 'arithmetic' vs 0.942 for '1'), but no method to predict or handle difficult targets
Evaluation metric concerns: ASR requires all action components within threshold ε, but ε not clearly specified; no sensitivity analysis for this critical parameter
Limited baseline comparison: Baffle is only directly comparable offline RL baseline; IMC from adversarial ML; missing comparisons with other recent RL backdoor methods

Hyperparameter sensitivity incompletely analyzed: multiple design choices (λ, MI-FGSM parameters, alternation frequency) lack strong justification; Table 19 shows performance varies significantly with alternation frequency

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Clearly identifies that TO models require fundamentally different attack approaches than traditional RL agents, with compelling motivation for post-training attacks
Comprehensive empirical investigation: Systematic exploration of target action selection, trigger dimensions, and reward manipulation effects provides valuable insights to the community
Extensive experimental validation: 540 unique experiments across 6 environments, 3 architectures, multiple seeds with thorough ablation studies and clear presentation of results
Strong empirical performance: Achieves 71.9% ASR with only 0.3% poisoning rate and superior benign task performance (0.914 BTP) compared to baselines
Excellent reproducibility: Source code provided with detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, and comprehensive appendices enabling full replication
weaknesses: Critical unsolved practical problem: Trigger dimension selection dramatically affects efficacy (Table 2: 0.915 vs 0.000 ASR) yet authors acknowledge 'lack of automated methods.' This fundamental challenge is never resolved, undermining practical applicability of the attack

Limited technical novelty: Trajectory filtering (simple length-based), batch poisoning (standard consistency approach), and alternating training (existing MI-FGSM + bilevel optimization from Pang et al. 2020) are incremental applications of known techniques

Target action selection unaddressed: Paper evaluates diverse targets but doesn't solve how attackers would select effective actions a priori (e.g., boundary vs. interior values differ by ~8.9x in ASR per Table 1)

Threat model limitations: Post-training attack requires knowledge of effective trigger dimensions; without dimension selection solution, adversary must either trial-and-error or have prior knowledge, reducing practical threat severity

Incomplete defense evaluation: Only fine-tuning is effective (requiring full retraining). Other defenses (pruning, activation clustering, spectral analysis) fail completely with no exploration of robust training or detection mechanisms specifically designed for TO models

Limited real-world applicability: Experiments restricted to low-dimensional D4RL tasks (11-59D states), no image observations, all Transformer-based models—generalization to real robotics and non-Transformer architectures unclear

Baseline comparison concerns: Baffle uses different threat model (data poisoning vs. post-training) and different poisoning rates (10% vs. 0.3%), making direct comparison problematic; IMC designed for adversarial perturbations, not backdoors

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: Why boundary actions succeed while interior values fail (fundamental property or dataset-specific?) is not analyzed; limited insight into trigger effectiveness properties; Section 4.2 lacks explanation of why MI-FGSM succeeds for trigger learning when other methods fail

strengths: First systematic study of action-level backdoor attacks on trajectory optimization models, identifying an important and practical security vulnerability
Comprehensive empirical investigation (540+ experiments) demonstrating effectiveness across diverse D4RL environments and multiple TO model architectures
Clear empirical evidence that trigger design matters critically while reward manipulation is ineffective for TO models, with well-designed ablation studies
Well-motivated practical threat model (post-training supply-chain attacks) that is increasingly relevant as TO models scale
Technically sound methodology combining trajectory filtering, batch poisoning, and alternating training with strong quantitative results (ASR=0.719, BTP=0.914, CP=0.701)
Substantial improvements over baselines (105% vs. Baffle on CP metric) while using dramatically lower poisoning rates (0.3% vs. 10%)
Thorough supplementary material including extensive defense evaluation, implementation details, and honest discussion of limitations and ethical considerations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in individual components: trajectory filtering is simple length-based filtering, batch poisoning straightforwardly duplicates and poisons batches, alternating training directly applies existing bi-level optimization from prior work
Critical unsolved problem: trigger dimension selection lacks principled solution; attempted gradient-based methods (Grad-CAM, NTK spectrum) failed completely, forcing reliance on random sampling
Limited theoretical understanding: intuitive explanations for why triggers supersede rewards, but no deep analysis of convergence properties, dimension importance, or architectural vulnerabilities

Evaluation scope incomplete: only continuous-state, continuous-action environments tested; image-based states not evaluated despite being practically important; generalization to other sequence models unclear

Defense evaluation concerning: most defenses completely fail, suggesting fundamental architectural vulnerability; fine-tuning works but requires strong assumptions; raises unresolved questions about TO model security

Hyperparameter sensitivity inadequately addressed: significant sensitivity to alternation frequency (Table 19), environment-specific tuning required (Appendix I), limited guidance for new problem domains
Inconsistent performance across tasks and models (ASR ranges 0.296-1.000) without systematic analysis of failure modes or predictability

Baseline comparisons not fully equitable: IMC designed for adversarial perturbations rather than backdoors; Baffle uses 10% poisoning vs. 0.3% for TrojanTO; missing comparisons with recent backdoor methods

ASR success threshold (ε = 0.01) appears arbitrary without justification; potential issues with BTP normalization when clean returns near zero; limited detectability analysis beyond behavioral metrics
